title_en: Is Grinding for Big Tech Still Worth It? Three Honest Years
excerpt_en: Three years into an operations job at a Shanghai tech giant, one 2023 graduate does the math: 200k earned, 200k spent, seventeen abnormal health results — and what AI changed in 2026.
body_en:
This article is adapted, with attribution, from the Bilibili video Ever More Competitive — Is Grinding for a Big Tech Job Still Worth It? Three Honest Years by UP host Yue Liang Zhu (Moon Pig): https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1QHsX6NEUL/. She graduated in 2023 and has spent three years in an operations role at a big internet company in Shanghai. Her question is one many people are asking: in 2026, is it still worth fighting your way into big tech?

A job that trades health for money

First, what the job actually is: extremely long hours, extreme psychological pressure and a wrecked body, in exchange for slightly higher pay and a life that is barely a life. The requirements: be efficient, always online, fluent with AI, aligned, multitasking, willing to work unpaid overtime, laptop in hand wherever you go.

And the people? At first everyone is a smart, polite, proactive, tough good student. Tough means: no matter how much pressure you pile on me, I still get the work done. It is as if the world's smartest, most usable people were penned up together to do work that is long and hard but means very little. The company is smart too: it squeezes this batch dry, then swaps in a newer batch that is even more usable and cheaper. The people who survive the grind slowly turn forceful, efficient, sharp-tongued — and contemptuous of anyone slower.

The money is real, but it doesn't stay

Big tech still has one thing worth wanting: money. For someone from a poor family, it is a visible road to accumulating wealth fast, especially in engineering roles.

But she is in operations. When she graduated in 2023 she took home 12,000 yuan a month, 200,000 a year — very low by Shanghai internet standards. Back then she firmly believed the money would only grow and effort would surely be rewarded. Now she says: how naive.

The problem was spending. In 2022, before graduating, she spent 40,000 yuan a year; after starting work, her yearly spending jumped straight to 200,000. The salary earned her nothing. Every day was just going to work and making videos, yet the money flowed away beyond control. Standing under the gleaming office towers, she felt like an ant in the city of Shanghai: the ground is scattered with honey, but you are still only an ant — and back in the suburbs, the suburbs are honestly more comfortable.

Beyond money, the perks are just icing: dress freedom, lots of young people, holiday gift boxes, a gym, a nice office, and mountains of internal information. With no pressure on, the place feels like a heaven of human intelligence, everyone producing heaps of documents every day, and a surprising one percent of it genuinely moves society forward. But time without pressure almost never exists.

The bill starts with your body

If you choose this job for money alone, the price that follows is enormous. When she was job-hunting she thought about nothing else: her family was poor, and she was fixated on proving she could earn, proving her degree and ability could be exchanged for a big-tech job. That obsession, she says, has ruined who knows how many people.

Once inside, the nightmare begins. First, the real exchange rate: the pay looks high but the hourly wage is not. Long hours, heavy workload, hard problems — you pour in nearly all your energy, doing the work of two or three people for one and a half people's pay. Then you notice every role seems equally miserable; nobody is not suffering, and every face looks tormented.

Then your degree quickly becomes a scrap of paper. A Peking University PhD started the same day she did; graduates of elite high schools are her colleagues — so what? Everyone is dragged equally into the same struggle, ranked only on output, efficiency, hours and attitude.

The body breaks first. Under chronic overwork you start to wonder whether you are spending your future life to earn money now — money earned, no life left to spend it. Her latest medical report just came out: seventeen abnormal results. The abnormalities do not shrink as her gym visits grow; they grow with her years of service.

Life breaks too. In her second year she realized she could not see the life she wanted in any colleague, nor in any manager. You can never climb your way into owning the company; the best you can become is a higher-grade beast of burden. Climbing costs enormously, and not climbing costs enormously too, because others will grind you to death. You can't out-grind them, and you can't lie flat either.

The springboard doesn't spring anymore

When you finally want to jump ship, you find the big-tech springboard doesn't work so well anymore. Roles at big companies are sliced extremely thin; you are a highly specialized screw. Your skills grow in a narrow band, switching fields is hard, and your options are few. After changing jobs she discovered several colleagues from her old company at the new one — each of them convinced they had made an unusual choice.

In 2026, AI lands another blow

All of the above was always true, but this year added new variables.

First, AI. Its arrival completely changed how she works, and made the skills she once relied on worthless — every single one, no exceptions. The higher her efficiency, the more work she gets; the more work, the higher the efficiency demanded. She calls herself a mysterious machine, and says this will grind her to death sooner or later.

Second, headcount is shrinking. Work that used to take an intern half a day is now done by AI in one prompt. This year's campus recruiting will most likely be even more brutal than 2023's. Her consolation to juniors: the year you graduate may matter more than all your effort.

Third, age. The industry keeps getting younger and more age-anxious. Three years in, she already counts as senior, and she is already planning for life after being optimized out. Her list of backup careers is long: tour guide, counselor, gym class coach, corporate-culture trainer, something in the pet industry, ride-hailing driver (no license yet), stand-up comedian. Sometimes she has nightmares that if she hasn't achieved something huge by 35, her life might as well be over.

Her five questions

Her way of deciding is to ask a few questions.

One: are you truly short of money? If yes, come. If your family has a little money, don't — go learn other ways of growing assets.

Two: do you know what you want? If not, come and experience it. If you have a clear goal for your life, don't come — why not go live that life directly?

Three: were you born to compete? Then come and fight; the gate is wide open for you.

Four: were you born with a weak body and low energy? Then don't come; you won't outlast anyone.

And for those who choose the money, her advice is to do the math in advance. Can you actually complete your primitive accumulation on this road? Will what you earn cover big-city living costs, the permanent damage to your body, the revenge spending that stress triggers, and the decades of mortgage you signed when your head wasn't clear? Priced that way, this job is not a positive-return choice for everyone. And not going to big tech is nothing to regret for a lifetime — no single decision ruins a life.

After the main quest, the sea

She has a new mindset now. First, cherish: she knows she can work, run a video channel, exercise, learn English and piano, and keep her household in order all at once; if she really wanted to grind, few could out-grind her. But she doesn't want to grind anyone, and if someone tries to grind her, she won't take the bait. A person is just borrowing a shell to experience the world; time is the real wealth, and where your time goes, there your life is. This job's deepest flaw is that it leaves no memories: three years since graduation feel like a single repeated day, and time and money both flowed away. So she will guard her time, energy and ability, and think hard about where to spend them.

Second, calm. Fresh and eager at the start, then struggling and fighting, and now only a long, endless calm. She understands more and more that work means nothing beyond the income it trades for; no mission or sense of worth will be found in it. She is calm about managers too: whether they pressure you, encourage you or train you, it is all just management technique for getting a task done.

The main quest — a degree, a job — she has played through, and she doesn't want to keep climbing the hard way. She has seen what is on top of the mountain. Now she wants to know what lies across the sea. The side quests of her life are only just beginning.
